questions.q: You want to know whether purchase rate differs across mobile, desktop and tablet sessions. Which test fits?
options: Chi-square test of independence on the device-by-purchase table of counts
Chi-square goodness-of-fit against a single number
questions.explain: Both variables are categorical and you have counts, so the chi-square test of independence on a contingency table applies.

questions.q: What does the chi-square statistic sum up?
options: Squared gaps between observed and expected counts, each divided by the expected count
questions.explain: chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected. Larger values mean the data diverge more from the null's expectation.

questions.q: In a device-by-purchase table with 3 device rows and 2 outcome columns, how many degrees of freedom does the independence test have?
The device-by-purchase test gave p = 0.0019, but Cramér's V was 0.079. How should you describe this?
options: A statistically detectable but small association
No association, because V is below 0.1
Proof that tablets cause more purchases
questions.explain: A small p says the association is unlikely to be chance; a small V says it is weak. Neither statistic establishes causation.

questions.q: A goodness-of-fit test on 300 tickets across five weekdays gives p = 0.327. What is the right conclusion?
options: The workload is proven to be perfectly even
The data don't show a departure from an even workload, though a small sample could hide moderate imbalances
The test is invalid because p is above 0.05
questions.explain: A non-significant result means no clear evidence against the null. It does not prove the null.
